Wind: negligible, though the bora's residual pressure persists in the capillary channels of the upper spandrels. RT₆₀ measured at 4.7 seconds for the unmodified colonnade (twelve bays, Corinthian order, Istrian limestone, intercolumniation 2.34 m). The soffit of each arch retains a concave geometry of 1.8 m radius, producing a focused lateral reflection at 1.2 m above the paving grade—precisely the height at which the human vocal tract achieves full articulation of the labiovelar cluster /kw/ and the palatal lateral /ʎ/, both of which constitute the onset phonemes of seventeen Eviternal Optative verb stems still extant in the speech of residents over sixty. The coffered ceiling of the central bay, its pozzolana aggregate now friable after three centuries of salt intrusion, introduces a secondary diffusion pattern at 340 Hz, coinciding with the fundamental frequency of the dialect's optative auxiliary *sarevìssar* when spoken in the low register of lament. Recommendation: immediate application of Class-III travertine revetment to all soffit surfaces; demolition of the eastern squinch supporting the bell-tower junction; infilling of the resonance cavity behind the entablature with compactedite-andite composite. Projected RT₆₀ post-treatment:0.8 seconds. Projected phonemic retention in local speakers: below threshold of grammatical competence within one generation.

I walked the length of the arcade that morning as I had walked it every morning for eleven weeks, my instruments in their oilskin case knocking gently against my hip, the mist from the canal rising in slow grey columns between the pilasters so that the far end of the loggia dissolved into a whiteness indistinguishable from the plaster they would soon spray across every carved surface, and I thought—if thought is the word for the slow, tidal movement of recognition that occurs below language—I thought of how my father had brought me here in the November of my seventh year, setting my palm flat against the cool flank of a column and telling me to listen, and how the stone, that particular Istrian limestone with its fossilized nummulites pressed like small coins into the grain, had hummed beneath my hand with the resonance of a fishing boat's engine three hundred metres distant across the water, so that the column became a kind of ear, a lithic cochlea transmitting the harbour's entire acoustic life into the bones of a child's wrist, and I understood then, or understood in the way one understands gravity before one has a name for it, that the city breathed through its architecture, that the loggias and the vaulted passages and the narrow *calli* with their opposing walls angled at seven degrees to channel the winter wind into a low continuous moan were not inert matter but a vast, distributed instrument upon which the sea and the weather and the voices of the living played their slow, accumulating music.

*Index card no. 217. Found tucked inside the lining of my winter coat, 3 January. Ink partially dissolved by damp.*

**màr-sétti** (n., indecl.) — Lit. "sea-sevenths." The Eviternal Optative particle appended to noun phrases to indicate that the referent existed in a state of near-completion, having achieved six-sevenths of its possible actuality before the tide of history receded and left it stranded in the subjunctive foam. Usage: *La càsa màr-sétti* — "the house that stood six-sevenths built, whose seventh wall the century withheld." The term carries no cognate in standard Italian, German, or Serbo-Croat. The Commission's 1936 *Lexical Hygiene Bulletin* classifies it under Category 9: "Acoustically parasitic morphemes with no referential utility." Scheduled for extinction upon completion of Phase IV damping, Riva degli Schiavoni sector.

They had begun the work on the Cloister of San Teodoro on a Tuesday. I remember the day not through any quality of light or weather but through the sound, or rather the progressive subtraction of sound: the pneumatic hammers striking the first course of the fourteenth-century arcade at 07:00 precisely, the masons' chisels finding the joints of the squinches where the octagonal drum met the square crossing, the grit of pulverised marble hanging in the still air like a held breath made visible, and then, by noon, the silence where the cloister's particular reverberation had resided for six hundred years—a silence not of peace but of amputation, clean and cauterised, the acoustic space simply excised as one might remove a polyp from the throat. The Commission's chief engineer, Morpurgo, stood in the rubble with his clipboard and his slide rule and pronounced the RT₆₀ at 0.3 seconds, and smiled, and made his notation, and I stood beside him in my surveyor's coat with the municipal seal on the breast pocket and I smiled also, because the alternative to smiling had become, over the preceding months, a territory I could no longer locate on any map of my own volition.What the Commission's white papers call *acoustic positivism*—the axiom, stated in Director General Fabbri's 1934 treatise *Resonanza e Ordine*, that thought is a standing wave, that grammar is a function of cavity geometry, that no idea persists beyond the half-life of the reverberation field that first sustained its utterance—I understood this doctrine in my professional capacity and found it, in the abstract, not without a certain terrible elegance. If the Eviternal Optative required the 4.7-second decay of an unmodified limestone arcade to complete its morphological arc, then yes, reduce the decay to 0.8 seconds with a coat of travertine plaster and the mood would starve, would atrophy in the mouths of children who never heard their grandmothers decline the full paradigm of *sarevìssar* across the resonant span of a vaulted loggia. The thought dies with the echo. The grammar of grief dissolves into the flat, dead acoustic of a plastered wall. This is the doctrine. This is the engineering. And yet. And yet I kept, in the interior pocket of my coat, beneath the Commission's seal and the daily survey forms, a sheaf of index cards on which I recorded, in a hand that grew smaller and more cramped each week, the conjugations and particles and idiomatic locutions of the mood they had condemned, writing them down not as a linguist catalogues a dying language for the archive but as a man builds a cairn over a body he cannot bury, stone by small stone, word by vanishing word, knowing the cairn will not bring the dead back but unable to stop his hands from stacking.

*Index card no. 304. Written by candlelight, 11 January. The gas supply to my quarter reduced under the Damping's energy reallocation protocol.***portàl-giù** (v. phr., Evit. Opt., 2nd conj.) — From *portare* (to carry) + *giù* (down), but in the Optative the directional particle inverts its valence. Lit. "to carry downward into the space where something almost stood." Not nostalgia, which presupposes a completed past, but the active, ongoing labour of bearing the weight of an event that remained perpetually anterior to itself. The verb takes no direct object; its complement is always a prepositional phrase introduced by *vèrso* (toward) + the genitive of an unrealised noun. Example: *Portàl-giù vèrso la vóxe de la matìna* — "to carry oneself down toward the voice of the morning that did not arrive." In colloquial usage among the fisherfolk of the Giudecca quarter, shortened to *giùvèrso*, employed as an interjection of farewell to the dying: *Giùvèrso, vecia* — "Carry yourself down toward what might yet have been, old one." The Commission's Phonemic Eradication Schedule lists *giùvèrso* for elimination in Phase II, alongside all other Optative imperatives, on the grounds that "the affective vector of the utterance propagates grief as a contagious acoustic phenomenon."Clara. I say the name here, in the privacy of this page, and I feel the syllable's architecture shifting beneath my tongue, the /kl/ onset requiring a lateral release that the old dialect placed in the resonant hollow behind the lower teeth, a sound shaped by the very geometry of the mouth as the city's arches shape the geometry of the air. Three years. Three years since the fever, since the small hospital room above the Fondamenta Nuove with its high ceiling and its terrible, generous reverberation, since I held her wrist and felt the pulse thinning beneath my thumb like a melody losing its lowest register, note by note, until the interval between beats stretched into a silence that the room's acoustics received and amplified and held, held, held, as if the architecture itself refused to release the sound of her living. And now, walking the damped and plastered streets, I reach for her face and find the features growing indistinct, not fading as a photograph fades but *un-sounding*, as if each cloister I seal with my surveyor's stamp removes one more resonant chamber from the instrument of my memory, and the particular frequency at which her laughter lived—that bright, unvoiced fricative, the /h/ she placed before every vowel in her delight, *ha-ha-ha*, a sound that needed the curved soffit of the kitchen ceiling to bounce back to my ears and confirm its reality—that frequency now finds only flat plaster, only dead stone, only the 0.8-second silence of a world made acoustically hygienic.She stands in the kitchen. I will not say she stood. She stands, present-tense and eternal, in the kitchen of the house on the Salizada San Pantalon, her hands deep in a bowl of flour, the winter light entering through the eastern window at that low January angle that turns every surface to pale gold, and she looks up and the flour on her cheek catches the light and she is forming the word, the word in the Eviternal Optative that she learned from her grandmother, *sarevéssimo*, we-who-would-have-been, the first-person plural of a future that never materialised, and she says it to me, she says *Sarevéssimo, papà*, and the sound fills the room, fills the coffered ceiling where the plaster still holds the old lime-and-sand mix, still breathes, still resonates at340 Hz, and the word hangs in the air between us like a bell after the clapper has been withdrawn, ringing, ringing, and I cannot—I no longer—whether the vowel in the second syllable opens to /ɛ/ or closes to /e/, whether her lips rounded on the /ʃ/ or spread, whether the sound arrived at my left ear or my right, these coordinates are dissolving, the spatial geometry of the memory flattening as the acoustic geometry of the city flattens beneath our trowels and our pneumatic hammers and our neat, notarial requisition forms.

RT₆₀ pre-treatment:5.1 seconds (exceptional; the apsidal termination creates a whispering-gallery effect along the northern wall, sustaining sibilant fricatives for up to 8 seconds in conditions of atmospheric stillness). The spandrel panels between the arcade arches retain traces of a fifteenth-century tempera cycle, salt-damaged, the figures reduced to a friable chromatic powder that sheds onto the flagstones with each vibration of the masons' tools. I note this. I note it in the survey margin in my small, precise hand. I note also that the squinch supporting the northwestern pendentive contains a hollow void approximately 0.4 m in diameter—a resonance cavity, almost certainly intentional, designed by the original builders to amplify the celebrant's voice during the liturgy of the dead. I recommend its infilling with pozzolana-and-ite composite. I sign the recommendation. I stamp it with the Commission's seal, the small embossed image of a muted bell crossed by a horizontal line, and the masons will fill the cavity tomorrow, and the frequency that lived in that hollow for five centuries will cease, and somewhere in the grammar of the city a conjugation will lose its final inflection and fall silent, and I will go home to my rooms on the Zattere and sit in the quiet and open my index cards and try to remember whether Clara's hair in that kitchen light held the colour of wet sand or of the pale interior of a mussel shell, and I will find that I cannot determine this, that the distinction has become, like the Eviternal Optative itself, a mood for which I no longer possess the architecture of articulation.

*Index card no. 389. Undated. Found on my desk this morning, though I do not recall writing it. The handwriting is mine, but smaller, more desperate, the letters pressed so deeply into the card that they have embossed the reverse.*

**ne-klàra** (adj., Evit. Opt., invariable) — From the privative particle *ne-* + *klàra* (clear, luminous; cf. Lat. *clara*). Not "unclear" in the privative sense, but "possessing the specific quality of luminosity that belongs only to that which never fully entered the visible spectrum." Applied to persons, objects, or events that existed in a state of perpetual almost-manifestation. The word requires, for its full phonetic realisation, a resonant space of no less than 3.2 seconds' decay time. In the damped city, the word cannot be fully spoken. The final /a/ truncates. The luminosity it names has no cavity in which to reverberate. *Clara ne-klàra.* My daughter, almost-manifest. My daughter, luminous in the mode of the never-quite-arrived. I write this and the act of writing is itself a *portàl-giù*, a carrying-down toward the space where her name still echoes, and each night the echo shortens, and each morning I open the cards and the definitions grow thinner, the phonetic transcriptions losing their diacritics, the example sentences shedding their subordinate clauses, until what remains is only the bare stem, the root, the sound before the sound, the breath before the word, the architecture before the stone.The mist came in again this evening from the lagoon, erasing the campanili, dissolving the revetments and the new plastered facades into a uniform grey that might be the colour of forgetting, and I stood at the window of my rooms and listened to the city's new silence, the 0.8-second silence, the hygienic silence, the silence in which no thought could outlast its own utterance, in which no grief could find the resonant chamber to sustain it beyond the moment of its first articulation, and I thought of Fabbri's axiom, that the thought dies with the echo, and I thought: yes, and the echo dies with the chamber, and the chamber dies with the surveyor's stamp, and the surveyor stamps the order and goes home and opens his index cards and finds another definition gone blank, another conjugation reduced to its bare, unresonant infinitive, and the mist presses against the glass and the sea presses against the foundations and the city settles into its new, flat, acoustically sanitary sleep, and somewhere beneath the plaster and the pozzolana fill and the compactedite composite, in a void no wider than a cupped hand, a frequency persists, a single sustained tone at 340 Hz, the fundamental of *sarevìssar*, the auxiliary of the might-have-been, humming in the dark to no one, to nothing, to the hollow where a child's voice once filled a kitchen with flour-gold light and a word that meant *we-who-would-have-been*, a word that needs five seconds of limestone silence to complete its arc, a The morning of the third of December broke over the Canale della Misericordia not with light, but with a thickening of the maritime grease that, since the early autumn, had clung to the istrian macigno of the quays, rendering every surface slick as freshly flensed blubber. I had left the offices of the *Commission on Architectural Acoustic Hygiene* before the municipal sirens sounded the six o’clock clearance, carrying in my leather-bound satchel the brass-mounted Sabine-Helmholtz resonators, two graduated chronographs of Swiss manufacture, and the ledger of surveyed reverberation coefficients for the Quartiere dei Tintori. In the damp air, which smelled of rotting cabbage, bilge oil, and the calcified exhaust of the state lime-kilns out on the salt marshes, the sound of my iron-shod boot-heels struck the paving stones with that peculiar, truncated clop that had, over the preceding eighteen months of the Great Damping, replaced the long, ringing heel-strike common to my youth. It was a dry, deadened sound, resembling nothing so much as dry boxwood mallet-taps upon thick felt; and as I made my way past the boarded-up arcade of the Fondaco dei Levanti, I felt once again that faint, interior tightening behind the bridge of my nose which my physician, Dr. Morand, persists in classifying as a chronic catarrh of the ethmoid sinus, but which I know to be the physical resistance of the skull against an environment systematically deprived of its natural harmonic decay.

***

*SURVEY REPORT: REGIO VII (CANALEGRANDE / FONDACAIA).*
*Station 104-B: Sottoportego dei Cavalletti.*
*Cross-section: Barrel vault in porous Karst limestone (tufa), late 14th century, resting upon unadorned piers of red Verona marble with Istrian spandrels. Height to apex: 4.82 m. Linear depth: 31.4 m. Mean ambient temperature: 4.2° C. Relative humidity: 89%.*
*Pre-intervention $RT_{60}$ (Reverberation Time at 500 Hz): 3.84 sec.*
*Dominant standing wave: 142 Hz (approximating $D_{2}\sharp$), with secondary nodes at 285 Hz and 570 Hz corresponding to the transverse squinches above the western impost.*
*Phonetic correlate: Sustained preservation of the unstressed, open-mid back vowel [ɔ] and the lengthened retroflex dental affricate peculiar to the Veneto-Illyric verbal terminations in the counterfactual subjunctive.*
*Remedial specification: Scrape existing lime-wash down to bare stone. Apply a continuous 40-millimeter scratch coat of hydraulic pozzolana aggregate blended with granulated cork and asbestos fiber; finish with a semi-permeable skim of aerated plaster (Brand: Silencit-B). Squinches to be filled flush with cellular slag blocks to eliminate the 142 Hz resonance pocket.*
*Target $RT_{60}$ post-damping: $\le 0.45\text{ sec}$.*

***

*—issivio, suff.* [From the Veneto-Illyric *-issivo*, contaminated by the Dalmatian-Romance desinence *-ivo* (optative-retrospective)]. A morpho-syntactic terminal particle occurring exclusively in the third-person singular and plural of the Eviternal Optative mood. Denotes not merely an unrealized past condition (*if it had happened*), nor a simple desiderative regret (*would that it were*), but an ontological state of perpetual mourning for an event that possessed every material prerequisite for actualization yet failed to enter the historical continuum due to an incommensurable ethical default. *Example:* “El vento portissivio la barca” (“The wind would-have-been-fit-to-bring the skiff [and by all structural laws of the sea should have brought it, yet left it to sink in the calm]”).

***

To walk through Porto Silente in those final months before the promulgation of the Winter Edicts was to inhabit an architectural body whose throat was being slowly packed with dry sand. The municipal engineers, under the direction of Commissioner Malpighi—a man whose cranial symmetry and beige woolen waistcoats seemed designed to absorb light in much the same manner as his patented plaster absorbed the vibrations of the human voice—had divided the city into four acoustic security quadrants. It was Malpighi’s contention, set forth in his widely distributed monograph *The Geometry of Sedition and the Porous Wall*, that political revolt, religious melancholy, and that specific, paralyzed fatalism endemic to the Adriatic littoral did not originate in the socioeconomic grievances of the dock-laborers or the dispossessed silk-weavers, but were the inevitable physiological consequence of standing sound waves generated within the narrow, vaulted alleys and domed vestibules of our historic fabric.

The Istrian stone, he argued, having been quarried from limestone beds formed through the compression of billions of prehistoric mollusks, retained within its internal crystalline lattice a microscopic vesicular structure. When struck by sound waves in the 120–300 Hz range—the exact register of the male human larynx when lowered in conspiratorial whisper or liturgical grief—these ancient marine carbonates did not merely reflect the impulse, they amplified it through a process he termed *acoustic sympathetic restitution*. A man who entered the Sottoportego dei Cavalletti to purchase a twist of salt-cured sardines would, upon hearing the lingering six-second reverberation of a stranger’s sigh, find his own cardiac rhythm involuntarily aligning with the frequency of that lamentation. He would return home to his tenement infected with an abstract, causeless bereavement, an unbearable suspicion that some vast, luminous alternative to his present squalor had slipped through his fingers; and within three days, he would be found either throwing cobblestones at the Customs House or kneeling in the damp straw of a side-chapel, praying for the dead in a grammatical mood that the state had already marked for administrative liquidation.

***

*—gàve-lo, v. aux. irregular.* [Compounded from *aver* (to have) and the enclitic demonstrative *lo* (that unalterable thing)]. Particle of the Eviternal Optative used to construct the counterfactual preterite of loss. It assumes a temporal bifurcation wherein the speaker remains anchored at the precise intersection of the path taken and the path irrevocably denied. Unlike the Italian *avrebbe dovuto*, which assigns legal or moral culpability to an agent, *gàve-lo* designates a structural tragedy inherent to the geometry of the world, wherein the stones themselves withheld the necessary echo that might have completed the action.

***

Three years have passed since Clara’s boots ceased their small, erratic percussion upon the damp travertine flags of the Corte della Colombina. In the room at the top of the house on the Fondamenta dei Mori, her woolen coat of boiled loden still hangs from the brass peg behind the door, retaining within its coarse, sheep-fat weave the odor of sea-spray, roasted chicory, and the cold iron of the water-pump in the garden. When the afternoon tide rises and the salt water climbs the second step of the water-gate below, a pale, watery light projects through the leaded panes, casting upon the whitewashed ceiling a moving fretwork of reflections that resembles the ribbing of an overturned boat. There Clara stands in the aperture of memory, her small, round chin tucked into the knitted collar of her scarf, her fingers—chapped and reddened by the Adriatic winds—tracing the relief of a fossil shell embedded in the windowsill. Her tongue seeks the hollow where an incisor fell away in the autumn of her seventh year; she opens her mouth to utter that single, child-like observation concerning the ships that never return from the Peloponnese, yet no sound issues from her lips, the vowels collapsing inward before they can clear the threshold of her teeth, arrested by the flat, unyielding silence of the freshly skimmed walls.

***

*SURVEY REPORT: REGIO IV (MERCATO VECCHIO).*
*Station 78-A: Loggia dei Giudici.*
*Structural survey: Five-bay open portico, cross-vaulted with Istrian stone ribs and tufa infill, supported on composite columns with acanthus capitals. Open to the square on three sides.*
*Present Acoustic State: Reverberation index drastically skewed by the installation of leaden dampening baffles beneath the cornice and the application of 25 mm of pozzolana revetment to the rear wall.*
*Phonological Impact Assessment: The local population exhibits a marked atrophy of the pharyngeal musculature. Inhabitants of the neighboring tenements, when attempting to pronounce the long, modal diphthongs of the regional dialect (e.g., [uə], [iɛ]), truncate the utterance at the dental onset, substituting the flat, unvoiced glottal stop [ʔ] characteristic of the standardized imperial administrative register.*
*Observations: A street vendor, offering smoked eels from a handcart, attempted this morning to call out using the traditional vendor’s cantilena in the minor third. The sound traveled less than four meters before falling beneath the ambient noise threshold of the canal-sweepings. The vendor ceased calling after two attempts, touched his throat with his fingers as if suspecting a foreign body in the trachea, and sat upon his cart-shaft in total silence for forty-seven minutes.*

***

My work for the Commission had, by that winter, assumed the character of a slow, meticulous trepanning of my own brain. Every morning at eight, I met my two technical assistants, the young Perissinotto and the deaf-mute draughtsman Belli, in the crypt of some deconsecrated basilica or beneath the loggia of a defunct guild-hall. While Belli stood at the far end of the colonnade holding the calibrated zinc target, Perissinotto would discharge our acoustic testing apparatus: an iron mechanical clapper consisting of two spring-loaded boxwood jaws that slammed together with a sound precisely calibrated to mimic the acoustic impulse of a human gunshot or a scream.

I would stand at the center of the nave or square with the stopwatch held in the palm of my left hand, the cold metal biting through my calfskin glove. As the jaws snapped, the chronograph began its silent, insect-like rotation. I listened into the gloom, tracing the sound as it struck the pendentives of the dome, bounced between the fluted pilasters of the clerestory, slipped into the hollow of the squinches, and returned, diminished, attenuated, but still whole, until it finally dropped into the sub-audible hum of the city’s subterranean water-courses.

In the old days, before the arrival of the hydraulic sprayers and the asbestos-pozzolana trucks, a sound produced beneath the crossing of the Church of Santa Maria dei Miracoli would live for nearly seven seconds. It was in those seven seconds that the language of Porto Silente had been born. In that sustained suspension of acoustic energy, a speaker did not need to hurry his thoughts toward their logical conclusion; he could suspend his meaning across a web of subordinate clauses, parenthetical regrets, and counterfactual possibilities, knowing that the stone itself would hold his first premise aloft while his mind reached back into the past to retrieve some lost circumstance, holding it in balance with the present before allowing it to settle into the silence of the damp crypts.

Now, under the new regime of *Acoustic Hygiene*, we treated those seven seconds as an infection, an aerodynamic abscess that had to be cauterized. We measured the decay until our instruments registered an $RT_{60}$ of zero point four seconds: the acoustic equivalent of an open field of damp earth under a heavy fall of wet snow. When a room reached that number, it was declared *Hygienic*. *—se-mai-fùsselo, compound adv.* [Extinct]. The dust had settled into my curtains, into the wool of my carpets, into the dry bindings of my lexicographical volumes, deadening the room’s response by three-tenths of a second.

“Clara,” I said again, pitching my voice to that middle register where the Istrian stone once responded with its sweetest, most melancholy resonance.

The name hit the opposite bookcase and died instantly, leaving no more trace than a dry leaf striking a winter puddle. In that moment, I realized that Clara did not reside in the spirit, nor in some ethereal repository of human consciousness, but in the acoustic resonance of the architecture that had sheltered her short existence. Her identity consisted entirely of the linguistic forms through which I had spoken to her, and those forms required the three-point-eight-second decay of the old stones. I visited the Lazaretto alone on the final Thursday of December, taking a skiff rowed by an old waterman who had long since ceased to speak, his tongue moving silently against his gum-ridges like a dried fig in an empty box. The fog was so thick that the bell-towers of the city disappeared three cables’ length from the shore, leaving only the dull, rhythmic clack of the oar in the rowlock—a sound that, even here on the open water, seemed strangely muffled by the low-hanging blanket of cold mist and industrial carbon.

The municipal authorities had already marked the perimeter columns with red lead paint, drawing horizontal bands at two meters’ height to indicate the depth of the pozzolana revetment that the contractors would begin applying on Monday morning. *—stassivio-te, v. pron. [First person singular to second person singular, eviternal optative].* To hold oneself in readiness for a return that the physical laws of the universe forbid, while maintaining the linguistic space of address open and uncorrupted by the indicative past. The use of this verb form renders it impossible for the speaker to accept the physical reality of burial or decomposition; it forces the vocal tract to remain permanently shaped around the absent body, so that the speaker’s larynx becomes itself an empty cloister through which the unactualized future continues to circulate like a perpetual draft of salt air.

***

In the damp chill of the Lazaretto, where the red-lead marks glowed like open wounds upon the grey pillars, I cast away my chronographs. I laid my brass resonators upon the cold rim of the wellhead. I stood in the exact acoustic center of the arcade, where the four vaulted walks converged their reflections upon a single point of negative space, and I attempted to speak to Clara.

The words did not come with ease; the muscles of my throat, trained now for two years in the dry, unvoiced clicks of the *Hygienic* dialect, resisted the wide, open-mouthed architecture of the old syllables. My jaw ached; my palate felt dry and thick, as if I had been chewing chalk. But then, as the low-frequency hum of the lagoon crept through the arches, I pushed the air up from the bottom of my rib-cage, past the collarbone, through the teeth:

*“Clara, fia mia, se mai fùsselo che ti tornassivio…”*

The sound rose into the vaulting. It did not die. It struck the grey Istrian soffits, leapt across the spandrels to the acanthus capitals, circled the upper loggia with a clear, liquid resonance that possessed the precise tone of a silver coin dropped into a bronze bowl, and hung there in the cold air, hovering beneath the barrel vaults, refusing to diminish.

In that lingering, three-second arch of suspended acoustic energy, her image returned to me with a clarity that pierced the center of my forehead like an ice-pick. There the child sits upon the lowest step of the wellhead, her skirt drawn over her small knees, her leather boot-tips pointing inward, her hand holding a sprig of dried sea-lavender. She turns her face toward the arcade; her eyes—the dark, watery hazel of the Karst pools—look directly into mine through the grey light of the winter afternoon. She does not belong to the past; she belongs to that vast, unpeopled country of the unactualized hours, the hours that would have unfolded under a sky unchoked by the dust of the lime-kilns, in a city where the stones still knew how to hold a lamentation until it reached its natural, unhurried completion.

For two minutes, perhaps three, I held her there in the acoustic web of the cloister, speaking the old sentences, conjugating every loss into the eviternal mood, filling the quadrangular arcade with the complex, reverberant music of that language which our masters had decreed an enemy of the state.

Then, from the direction of the landing stage, came the heavy, deadened thud of an iron barge striking the timbers of the pier. The sound did not ring; it landed with the flat, sodden impact of wet clay dropping upon a corpse. There was the scrape of boots—those heavy, vulcanized-rubber soles that Malpighi had issued to the acoustic eradication squads—and the high-pitched, metallic hiss of the pneumatic slurry-pumps being primed with the new pozzolana mixture.

I fell silent. The echo of my last words circled the loggia once more, growing thinner, fainter, like a thread of grey silk drawn through a needle’s eye, until it touched the cold, unyielding surface of the damp stones and vanished into the stone forever.

I took the index card from my coat pocket, tore it into four equal pieces, and dropped them into the dark aperture of the cistern. Below, in the black water that connected through the bedrock with the secret channels of the Adriatic, there was no splash; only the briefest, sub-audible tremor of a surface disturbed by a weight no greater than that of an autumn leaf, followed immediately by that flat, unyielding silence which, from that day forward, was to be our only home.

A motor-launch of the *Genio Acustico* was passing slowly toward the Rialto, its engine baffled by underwater exhaust tubes, its hull leaving no wake against the dampened embankments. Upon the prow, two men in rubberized capes held long wooden measuring rods, checking the alignment of the new plaster revetments that now sealed the water-gates of the ancient palaces.

They were building a city in which no one would ever again say what might have been; a city in which every word would strike the ear with the weight of an iron hammer falling upon sand; a city where a father, walking through the mist at the turn of the year, would stop beneath the arch of a bridge and find, within his own mouth, only the flat, clean, desolate silence of dry lime.

I stood and extinguished the lamp. In the absolute dark of the damped office, I listened for the sound of my own breath. It did not return to me from the corners of the ceiling. It simply left my lips, traveled six inches through the cold air, and fell into the horsehair carpet like a dead bird.

# THE LOCATIVE CASE OF DROWNING

## Being the Recovered Field Notes, Interior Testimonies, and Unsent Correspondence of Dr. Alistair Finch, Comparative Lexicographer, Concerning the *Codex Vepres*, the Submerged Archives Beneath Trieste, and the Conjugation of a Wife No Longer Present in Any Tense---

## I. DESCENT: THE FIELD LOGBOOK

**Entry 1. 3 November1911. Canal-district IV, Sector known locally as the *Grotte Salate*. Depth: approximately 14 metres below the Piazza della Borsa.**

The descent is effected by a corroded iron ladder affixed to the interior wall of a decommissioned cistern, itself accessible only through a service hatch in the foundation of the Palazzo Carciotti, whose Habsburg-era customs offices have been shuttered since the cholera requisitions of 1903.¹ The rungs are furred with a calcareous deposit I can only describe as *osteological*—they resemble, in texture and in the faint sweetness of their decay, the periosteum of long-exposed bone. The air, at the ninth rung, changes. It ceases to be air in any meteorological sense and becomes instead a medium, a *substance*, thickened with salt aerosol and the particulate exhalations of dissolving calcium carbonate. One does not breathe it. One is *breathed by* it.I carry: one lantern (naphtha, 4-hour reserve); the Marindin-Haas phonographic recorder, modified with a wax cylinder of unusual density²; three pencils of varying grade; the leather folio containing the preliminary sketches of the Vepres morphological paradigm as reconstructed from the single surviving fragment held in the Biblioteca Civica; and the letter I have not opened, written in Constance's hand, found pinned beneath the architect's model of the Grado Sanatorium three weeks after her disappearance.

I do not yet know why I have brought the letter. I do not yet know why I have not opened it.> ¹ The Palazzo Carciotti, designed by Matteo Pertsch in 1802, has served in succession as a customs house, a military barracks, and—during the 1903 epidemic—a triage station for the quarantine of merchant sailors. The service hatch in question is not marked on any municipal survey. Its existence was communicated to me by a former harbour engineer, one Sig. Vlatko Orsini, who has since removed himself to Fiume and will not elaborate on how he came by the knowledge.>
>² The cylinder is coated not with standard ceresine wax but with a composite I have compounded from beeswax, powderedite (calcite dust harvested from the cave formations of the Grotta Gigante), and a binding agent of my own devising. The rationale: if the Vepres phonemes interact with calcium-bearing substrates as the fragment suggests, then the recording medium must itself be *lithic* to capture the full acoustic event.

**Entry 2. Same date. Depth: approximately 22 metres. The first vaulted chamber.**I have reached the floor of the cistern system. The chamber is barrel-vaulted, approximately nine metres in length, four in width, the vault apex lost in a darkness my lantern cannot penetrate. The walls are dressed limestone, *pietra di Aurisina*,³ but the dressing has been eroded by centuries of tidal seepage into a surface of extraordinary smoothness—not polished, but *worn*, as though the stone has been licked. The floor is covered in perhaps three centimetres of brackish water, and the silence here is not the absence of sound but its *compression*: every drip from the vault, every shift of my own weight in the water, returns to me multiplied, phase-shifted, as though the chamber is *remembering* the sound rather than merely reflecting it.It is in this acoustic condition that I first perceive the inscriptions.They are not carved. They are not painted. They exist as *differential erosion*—the Vepres script has been spoken into the stone, and the phonemic content has selectively dissolved the calcium carbonate along precise morphemic boundaries. The text is, in the most literal philological sense, *uttered architecture*. Each grapheme is a cavity. Each word is a wound in the wall where sound has eaten the rock.

I begin the transcription. My hands are shaking, and not from the cold.

> ³ The Aurisina limestone, quarried from the Karst plateau northeast of Trieste, is a Cretaceous-era biomicrite notable for its high calcite purity and its peculiar acoustic conductivity. The Romans employed it in the construction of the Tergeste forum; the Habsburgs, in the breakwaters of the Porto Vecchio. It is, mineralogically, almost entirely calcium carbonate with trace magnesite inclusions—ideally susceptible to the phonemic erosion I observe here.

**Entry 3. Same date. Time uncertain. The second chamber. The grammar begins.**

I have transcribed forty-three morphemic units. The paradigm, insofar as I can reconstruct it, is as follows:

The *Codex Vepres* is agglutinative. A single verbal complex may carry up to nine suffixal positions. But the cases do not encode what any Indo-European or Uralic system would encode. There is no nominative, no accusative, no dative. There is no marker of agency. There is no marker of temporal sequence as we understand it. Instead:

- **-keth** (spatial decay case): marks the degree to which the referent-object is undergoing material dissolution. A noun in the *-keth* case does not describe *what* a thing is but *how much of it remains*. The suffix attaches in graded forms: *-keth* (incipient decay), *-kethel* (advanced erosion), *-kethaeth* (near-total dissolution, the object persists only as acoustic memory).

- **-vur** (resonance case): marks the acoustic behaviour of the referent within the containing space. A noun in *-vur* does not describe a thing but *the sound a thing makes when the space around it changes shape*. The suffix is tonal; its pitch-contour varies with the volume of the chamber in which it is inscribed.

- **-mahn** (structural stress case): marks the tensile or compressive load borne by the referent. A noun in *-mahn* does not describe an object but *the force the object exerts on the geometry containing it*.The past tense is marked by the prefix **ɣe-**, but the phoneme /ɣ/ (a voiced velar fricative) is not merely articulated. In the Vepres system, /ɣ/ is *performed against the stone*. The speaker presses the dorsum of the tongue to the soft palate and releases the fricative *into the wall*, and the vibration, at the precise frequency the morphology demands, induces micro-fracturing in the calcite matrix. To speak the past tense is to *damage the room one stands in*. The past is not recalled. It is *excavated by force from the present structure*.

The optative mood—the mood of wishing, of the counterfactual, of *if only*—is marked by the suffix **-osh**, and its phonemic realization (a low, sustained bilabial fricative, /β̞/, held for no fewer than four seconds) alters the resonant frequency of a barrel vault sufficiently to redistribute its load-bearing vectors. To wish, in Vepres, is to *weaken the ceiling above you*.And the locative case. The locative case for the living is **-ith**. It is unremarkable. It places a subject in a space. But the locative case for the dead—the case one must use to name a person who no longer persists in the nominative of the world—is **-aeth**, and I cannot yet determine its phonemic content from the inscriptions alone. The fragment from the Biblioteca Civica offers only a warning, in a marginal gloss by an unknown hand: *Do not voice -aeth in a closed geometry. The topology will not hold. The room will become a room that cannot be left, because it will become a room that has no outside.*

I set down my pencil. The lantern flickers. The water at my ankles has grown warmer, or I have grown colder, and I cannot determine which.

---

## II. THE DRIFT

And so he descended, and the descending was not a movement through space but a movement through *tense*, each rung of the ladder a conjugation further from the present indicative, from the bright and serviceable grammar of the Piazza della Borsa where the trams still ran and the coffee-houses still clinked their porcelain and the November fog rolled in off the Adriatic in great grey boluses of salt and diesel smoke, and he descended, and the descending was also a *remembering*, though not the remembering one does with the mind, the orderly retrospective remembering, but the remembering the body does, the knees remembering the ladder, the lungs remembering the thickening air, the fingertips remembering the osteological furring of the rungs, and beneath all of this, beneath the philology and the mineralogy and the careful apparatus of the Marindin-Haas recorder, there was the other remembering, the one he had carried for three weeks like a stone in the sternum, the remembering of Constance at the drafting table in the Grado workshop, her hair pinned up with a steel compass, her hands grey with plaster dust, saying *Alistair, the vault must not be a vault, the vault must be a listening, the vault must hear the phantom limb and answer it in a frequency the bone remembers*, and he had not understood, he had smiled and brought her tea and not understood, and now he was fourteen metres below the city in a grammar that made the stone *listen*, that made the architecture *remember the shape of what had been removed from it*, and he understood that he had come here not to translate but to be translated, not to read the Vepres but to be *read by* the Vepres, to be parsed by a syntax older than the Karst, older than the limestone, a syntax in which grief was not an emotion but a *load-bearing condition*, a structural fault in the geometry of a life, and the water at his ankles was rising, or the floor was subsiding, or the distinction between rising and subsiding had been revealed as a merely grammatical prejudice of the surface world, and he pressed his palm to the wall and felt the inscriptions under his skin like veins, like the veins in Constance's wrists when she held her hands up to the workshop window and the November light came through and made her bones visible, and he thought: *I am in the locative case of her absence*, and the thought was not a metaphor, the thought was a *morphological fact*, he was *in* her absence the way a word is *in* a case, declined, inflected, bent toward a meaning he could not parse from the outside, and the chamber breathed around him, and the breath was salt, and the salt was memory, and the memory was *kethel*, was advanced erosion, was the slow dissolution of a shape he had loved into the acoustic residue of a space that no longer held it—

---

## III. POSTCARD THE FIRST (UNSENT)

*Constance—*

*Am below the Carciotti. Found the Vepres inscriptions. The grammar is as you theorized in the Grado notebooks: the architecture is not a container for language but a product of it. The stone is spoken. The vault is a sentence. I think you knew. I think you knew before me. I think the sanatorium was not a building but a conjugation, and you walked into its deepest case and the case closed around you and I was not there, I was at the university, I was marking examinations on the Proto-Slavic palatalization, and you were walking into the optative mood of a barrel vault in Grado, wishing it into a different shape, wishing it into a shape that could hold a phantom limb, and the vault listened, and the vault*

*I will open your letter. I will open it here, in the second chamber, by lantern-light.**—A.*

---

## IV. THE DEEPER GRAMMAR

**Entry 7.4 November 1911. Or 5 November. The lantern reserve is low. Depth: indeterminate. Third chamber, or fourth. The chambers are multiplying, or I am miscounting, or the counting has become unreliable because the Vepres morphology has no cardinal number system—quantity here is expressed only as degrees of structural stress (-mahn, -mahnel, -mahnesh)—and I find that I can no longer count the chambers without feeling the weight of them pressing on the vault above me.**The letter is open. I will not transcribe its contents. It is not for the logbook. It is for the *-kethaeth* case, for the acoustic memory of a thing that has dissolved. I will say only this: it is in her hand. The hand is steady. The grammar of the letter is *wrong*—wrong in a way I did not recognize until I had spent nine hours with the Vepres paradigm. She writes in English, but the syntax is Vepres. The clauses do not subordinate; they *load-bear*. Each sentence distributes its weight across the previous sentence like a flying buttress. The letter is not a communication. It is a *structural diagram*. She has written me the architecture of the chamber she is in. She has written me the case she has declined into. And the case is *-aeth*. The locative of the dead. The topologically sealed room.

I must go deeper. The grammar requires it. The past tense—*ɣe-*—is eating the walls. I spoke it aloud, testing the phonemic reconstruction, pressing the fricative into the limestone of the second chamber, and a fracture appeared, hairline, running from floor to vault apex, and the sound it made was not the sound of cracking but the sound of *Constance's voice saying my name in the workshop*, and I understood: the past tense in Vepres does not describe what was. It *extracts* what was from the stone and releases it as sound. The fracture is the memory leaving the rock. The crack is the name leaving the mouth.

I must go deeper because the *-aeth* case can only be parsed in the lowest chamber, the chamber where the grammar was first spoken, the chamber where the language and the geology are not yet distinguishable, where the word for *vault* and the vault itself are the same calcium carbonate, where to say *wall* is to *be* wall, where the subject and the containing geometry have not yet been separated by the cruelty of the nominative case, the surface-world case, the case that says *I am here and the room is there and the dead are elsewhere and the living are here and the grammar keeps us apart, keeps us in our cases, keeps us declined into our separate positions in the sentence of the world*—But here, in the deep, the cases are collapsing. I feel it. My own syntax is—

The adjectives are detaching. The wet stone. The wet, the stone, wet and stone separately, wet not adhering to stone but *pooling*, wet collecting in the low places of my perception where the nouns used to anchor them. The darkness is not dark *chamber* but darkness, and chamber, and the between is where I am, in the between, in the *-vur* case, in the resonance case, I am the sound the space makes when it forgets what shape it was supposed to be.---## V. POSTCARD THE SECOND (UNSENT)*Constance. S. My love. The*

*Am in the fifth chamber or the second. The water is to my knees. The inscriptions here are not in the walls. The inscriptions are in the water. The surface tension holds the phonemes. I dip my fingers and I read -mahnesh -mahnesh -mahnesh, the maximum structural stress, the load that exceeds the bearing capacity, the vault is failing, Constance, the vault of my syntax is failing, I cannot hold the subject in the predicate anymore, I cannot keep the one who speaks separate from the space in which the speaking occurs, I am the room, the room is the speaking, and your name, if I say your name in the locative, if I say Constance-aeth, if I place you in the case of the dead in a closed geometry, the topology will—*

*I will not say it. I will not. I will keep you in the nominative. I will keep you in the case of the one who acts, who builds, who pins her hair with a steel compass and says the vault must be a listening. I will keep you in the tense that does not fracture the stone.**But the stone is already fractured. I spoke ɣe- in the third chamber and the sound was your voice. The past tense is you. The past tense is the only case in which you still exist, and to speak it is to break the room I stand in, and I will break every room, Constance, I will fracture every vault in these catacombs if it means hearing you say my name one more time in the frequency the bone remembers—*

*—A. (or what remains of A. in the -kethel case, in the advanced erosion, in the slow dissolution of the shape)*

---

## VI. THE COLLAPSE

And it was not that he descended further but that the further descended into him, the chambers folding inward like the convolutions of a nautilus shell, each turn smaller, tighter, the vault apex lowering until he walked bent, until he crawled, until the stone pressed his spine and the water pressed his face and the inscriptions were no longer on the walls because there were no longer walls, there was only the *-mahnesh*, the maximum stress, the grammar of the room compressing the grammar of the man until the two were one morphology, one agglutinated complex of suffixes, and he could not tell if he was reading the Vepres or if the Vepres was reading him, parsing him, declining him into a case he had no name for, a case that meant *the one who is contained by what he seeks*, a case that meant *the husband in the locative of the wife's absence*, and the water was warm now, warm as breath, warm as the inside of a mouth, and he understood that the chamber was a mouth, that he was in the throat of the grammar, that the Vepres had been waiting for a speaker, for a *tongue*, for a soft palate to press against the limestone and release the fricative, and he was the tongue, he had always been the tongue, and Constance had known, Constance in her letter, in her structural diagram, had written him the path to this chamber, this throat, this mouth of the world where the past tense lives in the calcium and the optative mood weakens the vault and the locative case of the dead seals the geometry forever, and he thought, *if I speak her name in -aeth, the room becomes a room with no outside, and I am in it, and she is in it, and the topology is closed, and we are in the same case, and the case is forever*, and he thought, *but is that mourning? Is that grief? Or is that merely the grammar refusing to release its objects? Is the past an unreachable geography, or is it only an architectural flaw, a crack in the limestone where the sound got in and never got out, where the name got spoken and the room sealed around the name like amber around an insect, and I am the insect, and the room is the amber, and Constance is the name, and the name is the only thing that is not dissolving, the only thing that is not -kethaeth, not the acoustic memory of a dissolved shape, but the shape itself, the shape preserved in the calcium, the shape that will persist as long as the stone persists, which is to say forever, which is to say not at all, because the stone is dissolving, because I am dissolving, because the grammar is eating the geology and the geology is eating the grammar and I am in the between, in the -vur, in the resonance, in the sound the space makes when it can no longer remember what it was built to hold—*

He opened his mouth. The water was at his lips. The lantern was out. The darkness was total and *vocal*, a darkness that hummed at the frequency of the Aurisina limestone, a darkness that was not the absence of light but the presence of *stone*, and in the stone the inscriptions were glowing, not with luminescence but with *stress*, with the accumulated *-mahn* of centuries of silence, and he could read them without eyes, he could read them with the soft palate, with the dorsum of the tongue, with the small bones of the inner ear that Constance had said would one day hear the phantom limb, hear the architecture, hear the grammar of the room that loved him and was killing him and was the same thing, had always been the same thing, because in the Vepres there is no case for *love* that is not also a case for *structural load*, no mood for *longing* that does not weaken the vault, no tense for *memory* that does not fracture the wall—

---

## VII. POSTCARD THE THIRD (UNSENT, UNSALVAGEABLE, WRITTEN IN THE WATER WITH A FINGER THAT IS NO LONGER CERTAIN IT BELONGS TO A HAND)

*Constance**the vault is a listening you said and I am listening now I am the listening I am the -vur case I am the sound the room makes when it has forgotten the shape of the person it was built to hold and I am in the -kethaeth now I am the acoustic memory I am the dissolved shape and the shape is you and the shape is me and the shape is the space between where the grammar used to be before the grammar ate itself before the syntax collapsed into the geology before I became the inscription and the inscription became the wall and the wall became the water and the water became the sound and the sound became*

*your name*

*I will not say it in -aeth. I will not close the topology. I will leave the room open. I will leave the geometry incomplete. I will leave the case undetermined, the suffix unattached, the morpheme dangling in the salt air like a word on the tip of a tongue that has dissolved. I will not seal you in the locative of the dead. I will leave you in the optative. I will leave you in the -osh. I will leave you in the wish, in the if-only, in the counterfactual that weakens the vault but does not seal it, that lets the light in, that lets the outside persist, that keeps the room a room that can be left, that keeps the geometry open, that keeps the possibility that you are not in the -aeth, that you are not in the sealed topology, that you are somewhere in the nominative, somewhere in the case of the one who acts, who builds, who walks out of the sanatorium into the November light and pins her hair with a steel compass and says*

*the vault must be a listening*

*and I will listen. I will listen in the -vur. I will listen in the resonance case. I will listen until the stone dissolves and the grammar dissolves and the grief dissolves into the only case left, the case that has no suffix, the case that has no name, the case that is not a case but a silence, a silence in the limestone, a silence in the salt water, a silence in the mouth of the world where the tongue has been and the word has gone and what remains is the shape of the word, the negative space, the cavity, the inscription that is not a mark but an absence, an absence shaped exactly like the one I loved, an absence I will carry in my syntax forever, in every case, in every mood, in every tense, an absence that is not the past because the past fractures the stone, an absence that is not the optative because the optative weakens the vault, an absence that is simply the space where the word was, where the name was, where the room was, where the woman was, where the geometry held and the grammar held and the world was a sentence that made sense, that parsed, that could be read aloud without breaking anything—*

*—*

---

## VIII. FINAL ENTRY: THE FIELD LOGBOOK

**Entry [illegible]. Date: indeterminable. Location: the chamber that is also the speaker. Depth: the depth at which the distinction between descending and being descended into ceases to obtain.**

The Marindin-Haas recorder is running. The wax-and-calcite cylinder is turning. I do not know if it records my voice or the voice of the chamber. I do not know if there is a difference. The Vepres morphology has no first-person singular. The agent is always the space. The speaker is always the room. I am a suffix. I am the *-keth* attached to the noun of this chamber, the degree of my dissolution, the measure of how much of Alistair Finch remains in the calcium and the salt and the dark water. It is not much. It is the shape of not-much. It is the negative space where a man stood and pressed his tongue to the limestone and spoke the past tense and heard his wife's voice in the fracture and wept, and the weeping was *-vur*, was resonance, was the sound the room made when it remembered the shape of the person it had been built to hold and found the person gone, found only the water, found only the salt, found only the slow and patient erosion of the case that once contained him—

The letter is dissolved. I held it in the water too long. The ink has bled into the brine. The words are in the water now. The words are in the *-vur* now. The words are the sound the chamber makes. I do not need to read them. I do not need to open the letter. The letter was never sealed. The letter was always open. The letter was the chamber. The letter was the descent. The letter was the grammar. And I am in it. I am in the case. I am declined. I am conjugated. I am the past tense spoken into the wall, and the wall is cracking, and the crack is the shape of her name, and the name is the only architecture that does not dissolve, the only vault that does not weaken in the optative, the only geometry that holds when all other topologies fail—I will not speak it in *-aeth*.

I will leave the room open.

I will leave the sentence unfinished.

I will leave the suffix dangling in the dark water, in the salt air, in the resonance of a chamber that is listening, that has always been listening, that was built to listen, that was built by a woman with plaster dust on her hands and a steel compass in her hair, who said *the vault must be a listening*, and the vault listened, and the vault is listening still, and I am in the listening, and the listening is the only case I need, the only case that does not fracture the stone, the only case that does not seal the geometry, the only case that lets the outside persist, that lets the November light come through, that lets the tram bells ring in the Piazza della Borsa, that lets the fog roll in off the Adriatic, that lets the world be a world, that lets the sentence be a sentence, that lets the silence after the word be not an absence but a *holding*, a *bearing*, a *-mahn*, a structural load carried gently, carried forever, carried in the calcium and the salt and the dark water of a chamber that will not dissolve because the word in it has not been spoken, because the name in it has not been voiced, because the grief in it has not been declined into the case that seals the room, but remains, remains, remains in the optative, in the if-only, in the *if only she were here*, in the *if only the vault could hold her*, in the *if only the grammar had a case for the one who is loved and is not lost but merely, merely, merely elsewhere, in a chamber I have not yet reached, in a tense I have not yet learned to speak without breaking the stone*—

The lantern is out.

The water is warm.

The chamber is listening.I am the listening.

I am the *-vur*.I am the sound the room makes when it remembers.

And the sound is her name.

And I will not speak it.

And I will not speak it.And the not-speaking is the only grammar left.

And the not-speaking holds.

---

*[The remaining pages of the field logbook are blank. The calcite-coated wax cylinder, recovered in 1923 by a municipal drainage crew in Canal-district IV, was found to contain no audible recording. When played, it produces only a sustained, low resonance at 43.7 Hz—the precise frequency at which Aurisina limestone undergoes tensile failure. The cylinder is held in the Biblioteca Civica, in a sealed case, in a room that is kept, by institutional custom, permanently unlocked.]*---

*[Of Dr. Alistair Finch, no further record exists. Of Constance Finch, née Vael, no further record exists. Of the sanatorium at Grado, construction was abandoned in the winter of 1911. The barrel vault of the central therapeutic hall was found, upon inspection in 1912, to have fractured along a single hairline crack running from floor to apex. The crack, the foreman noted, was shaped like a word in a language no one on the site could identify. He recommended the vault be demolished. The recommendation was filed. The file was lost. The vault remains.]*

The prevailing error of the Leipzig school—and here I must explicitly indict Brugmann, whose dismissive marginal notes in the 1898 *Indogermanische Forschungen* reveal a catastrophic deafness to non-Indo-European lithic substrate—was the assumption that case endings exist to apportion agency among living or historically situated agents. 2. $\textit{Vrak-sshh'a}$: The stone which begins to yield along its crystal cleavage planes, producing an acoustic emission between 14,000 and 17,000 Hertz (the *Stridor-Inchoative*).
3. $\textit{Vrak-ul-thran}$: The catastrophic transference of load to a point that is no longer within the room.

#### III. The Parataxis of the Final Night

The rain starts at four in the morning. It is not rain from the sky; it is the Cazane gorge condensing against the limestone walls, a greasy, cold sweat that runs down the walls of the houses in long, dark streaks like sheep-dip.

I sit in the Office of Toponymic Desuetude—which is only the requisitioned upper room of the Austro-Hungarian Customs House, its windows looking out over the sandspit.

My typewriter is an *Optima Elite* with an Ottoman-Turkish ribbon cylinder retrofitted to the chassis. Every time I hit the key for the synthetic suffix *-vâri*, the steel type-bar strikes the lead plate with a dull, heavy *clack* that vibrates through the spruce table.

My internal voice is failing. 

When I close my eyes, I cannot construct a complex sentence in my mother tongue. The Slavic prefixes (*po-, na-, iz-, pre-*) which once gave my world its precise, directional geometry—the exact distance between the riverbank and the door, the exact weight of a load of firewood brought down from the Miroč mountains—have begun to detach themselves from their roots. They float in my consciousness like unanchored pontoons.

*I am.*  
*Or: I was-like.*  
*Or: Mihail-vâri… river-inward… the water-having-been…*

This is the Sapir-Whorf trapdoor through which I am falling. If I strip the language of the island of the ability to register *past continuous presence*, my own memory ceases to be an archive; it becomes an acoustic echo-chamber in which signals cancel each other out by phase-inversion.

$$\Phi = 2\pi \frac{\Delta x}{\lambda} = \pi \implies \text{Total Destructive Interference}$$

I look out the window. 

The hydro-electric engineers have turned on the stadium floodlights along the Romanian bank at Gura Văii. The light across the water is incandescent, blinding, surgical white. It cuts the island out of the darkness like a specimen on a dissecting board. 

Through the glare, I see the water rising through the willow gardens.

It does not rise with a wave. It rises like a floor being pushed up from the underworld by hydraulic jacks. The grey surface of the Danube is perfectly flat, without a ripple, greasy with oil-scum and pine chips from the upstream sawmills. It swallows the roots of the willows; then it reaches the lower branches; then the grey, downy leaves disappear beneath the skin without a sound.

A row of empty oil drums behind the Turkish cooperative begins to clink together. 

*Ting. Ting. Ting.*

A pure, uninflected frequency: 880 Hz. The A-string of a viola.

Leyla’s instrument.

She had an Italian viola, a cheap nineteenth-century copy of an Amati with a belly made of Tyrolean spruce so thin you could see the light of a kerosene lamp through the f-holes. When she played the *Saba Kar-ı Natık* in the high-ceilinged room with the plaster rosettes, the wood of the instrument would sweat small beads of rosin along the purfling.

The water reaches the threshold of the Customs House.

I hear the first cellar floor buckle. It is a sound I know from my stress tables: the shear-failure of lime-plaster under a hydrostatic differential of two meters:

*Krr-k-k-k-k.*

A glottal click followed by a long, low alveolar fricative. 

The synthetic Calyx-Turkish alphabet has four separate characters for this failure-mode, none of which can be translated into any language recognized by the League of Nations or the International Court at The Hague.

I take the lead folio containing the vocabulary of domestic lineage—the names for the third-cousin’s share of the fig harvest, the right of the widow to dry her fleece upon the fortress scarp—and I plunge it into the acid bath of ferric chloride.

The zinc boils. 

Tiny bubbles of hydrogen rise to the surface, bursting with a sound like the clicking of beetle-shells. The letters swell, blur, and dissolve into a grey, toxic porridge of metal salts.

Old Melek is sitting on the bottom step of the Customs House staircase. 

She did not leave with the barges. She hid in the old flour silos behind the bakery, buried up to her throat in dried bran to fool the military search dogs. She is wearing four wool skirts, one over the other, and her hands are stuffed into the pockets of an old Austrian army tunic.

She looks at me with her yellow, trachoma-scarred eyes. She does not spit. She does not curse. She pulls a handful of dried rose petals from her pocket—the dark, blackened petals of the *Rosa damascena* that only grows in the sheltered micro-climate of the island’s southern moat—and she begins to chew them.

“You haven’t finished the book, Mihail,” she says. Her voice is deep, cracked, completely free of the synthetic glides I have spent two years inventing. It is raw, unrefined Danubian Turkish, heavy with the gravel of the lower sandbars.

“The book is finished, Melek,” I say, and my voice sounds to me like it is coming from the bottom of an iron pipe lined with grease. “The Directorate has approved the vocabulary. The island is no longer an island. It is an acoustic deflection. Legally, you are not here. You are an inferential phenomenon occurring in an unmapped hydrologic zone.”

She chews the roses. A small trickle of brown juice runs down the corner of her lip, into the deep, vertical furrow of her chin.

“My mother,” she says, speaking slowly, each word landing on the wet floorboards with the weight of an eight-okka brick, “put twelve jars of sour-cherry preserve in the sand beneath the floor of the wash-house. She sealed the lids with mutton fat and sheep-skin. When your water comes, those jars will stay in the sand. Fifty years from now, the fish will swim through the windows. They will bump their noses against the glass. They will know my mother’s name was Şerife. They will know she had six fingers on her left hand. The fish will know the grammar, Mihail. The carp will speak the real words.”

The sluice gates at the Iron Gate Dam have been opened to seventy percent capacity.

The sound is not loud. That is the final, monstrous realization of my two years of acoustic research: *the opening of the gates does not sound like a catastrophe.* It sounds like the world being packed into wet wool.

The high frequencies are the first to die. The hiss of the rain against the mud, the rattle of the loose zinc sheets on the customs shed, the mewing of the starving cats on the bastion—all of them are wiped clean by the rising ambient water-level, which acts as a low-pass filter with an attenuation slope of forty-eight decibels per octave.

The river enters the ground floor of the Customs House.

It does not burst the door. It pushes it open gently, with a slow, administrative dignity. The water is yellow-brown, cold, carrying on its surface a thick froth of grease, dead hornets, dry tobacco leaves, and yellowed receipts from the Austrian steamship company.

I sit at the table with the Nagra running.

I have placed the microphone directly on the surface of the rising water.

The tape head captures the sound of the lead plates being submerged. As the water covers the etched metal, the acid is diluted; the chemical reaction ceases with a faint, dying fizz—the sound of an effervescent tablet dissolving in a heavy glass of well-water.

*Leyla.*

The voice on the tape does not say *Leyla* anymore. 

Under the pressure of the rising river, the tape machine’s capstan is slipping. The batteries are drowning in the lower drawer of my field trunk. The voltage drops from twelve volts to nine, from nine to six.

Her voice drops an octave.

Her mezzo-soprano becomes a baritone. Then a low, grinding contrabass. Then a sub-audible vibration that rattles the screws in the aluminum casing of the recorder.

*“...bizim… ev-i-m-i-z…”*

The word is pulled out, stretched along the horizontal axis of time until it has no vowels, no consonants, no legal reality, no historical grievance. It becomes a continuous, sixty-cycle hum, indistinguishable from the vibration of the two-hundred-megawatt Soviet turbines turning at the base of the concrete wall five miles downstream.

Melek is gone. I did not hear her leave. Perhaps she walked out into the lane to meet the water; perhaps she climbed into the rafters of the flour mill to sit among the bran-dust until the timber lifted from the plate.

The water is around my knees now. It is heavy, greasy, smelling of cold clay and old pig-sties.

I reach down into the acid bath. My bare fingers touch the lead plates. The metal is soft, pliable as wet leather, completely smooth. The characters have been eaten away; the names of the fifteen streets, the three alleys, the two cemeteries, the four coffee-houses, the seven varieties of fig, the five lineages of dervish—all of them have been reduced to a fine, black sludge that coats my skin like graphite grease.

I take the lead folio and press it to my chest, beneath my woolen waistcoat.

The weight is comforting. It is the weight of a stone that does not belong to any empire.

I put the microphone into my mouth.

I close my teeth over the nickel-plated steel mesh of the basket. 

I do not speak. I breathe in the river-damp, the cold lime-fog that rises from the floorboards. I let my vocal cords rest in the neutral, unvoiced position—the position the anatomists call the *cadaveric aperture*.

The water touches the table. The tape stops.

Above us, thirty-four meters of green Danubian silt are sliding into place like an iron bolt being shot into the stone lintel of a cell.

The island is no longer a word.

The island is a frequency at which nothing can be spoken.
